Introduction

The project, LSM-Tree Storage Engine over Object Storage, aims to develop a simplified key-value storage system that combines the write-efficient Log-Structured Merge-Tree (LSM-Tree) architecture with scalable object storage.

The system will support basic key-value operations such as PUT, GET, and DELETE. Incoming writes will first be recorded in a Write-Ahead Log (WAL) and stored in an in-memory Memtable. Once the Memtable reaches a specified threshold, its contents will be converted into sorted, immutable SSTable files and uploaded to object storage.

The project will also implement background compaction to merge SSTables, manage outdated values, and improve read efficiency. A Virtual Lab website will provide an interactive interface for users to execute operations, observe storage files, and understand how the engine works.

The feasibility study evaluates whether the storage engine and its interactive demonstration can be implemented within the available technical resources and project timeline.

Problem Statement

Conventional storage systems face challenges when handling large volumes of data while maintaining efficient writes, reliable recovery, and manageable storage requirements. Writing every small update directly to remote object storage can introduce significant network latency and request overhead.

An LSM-Tree addresses the write problem by buffering operations in memory and periodically organizing them into larger, sorted files. However, combining an LSM-Tree with object storage introduces additional challenges, including remote read latency, SSTable management, metadata consistency, crash recovery, and compaction.

The project aims to address these challenges by developing a simplified storage engine that efficiently organizes key-value data, persists SSTables in object storage, and demonstrates its internal operations through an interactive Virtual Lab website.

Objectives and Scope

3.1 Objectives

  • Implement a key-value storage engine supporting PUT, GET, and DELETE operations.
  • Develop a WAL and Memtable to handle writes and support crash recovery.
  • Generate sorted, immutable SSTable files when the Memtable reaches a specified threshold.
  • Integrate an object storage service or compatible local emulator for persistent SSTable storage.
  • Implement basic compaction to merge SSTables and manage obsolete values and tombstones.
  • Maintain metadata to identify active SSTables and support recovery.
  • Develop an interactive Virtual Lab website to demonstrate storage operations and visualize the engine's behaviour.
  • Evaluate the system using performance measurements and correctness tests.

3.2 Scope

The project will focus on a single-node prototype and an educational demonstration interface.

Included in scope:

  • Basic key-value operations.
  • WAL-based recovery.
  • Memtable management and SSTable generation.
  • Object storage upload and retrieval.
  • Basic indexing and compaction.
  • Storage file visualization through the Virtual Lab.
  • Testing, benchmarking, and deployment of the demonstration website.

Outside the initial scope:

  • Distributed multi-node operation.
  • Production-grade database functionality.
  • Advanced compaction strategies and extensive caching optimizations.
  • Full production-level concurrency and fault-tolerance guarantees.

Proposed System and Architecture

The client sends operations to the storage engine. Writes are recorded in the WAL before being acknowledged, subject to the configured persistence guarantees, and then applied to the Memtable. When the Memtable reaches its threshold, the system generates an SSTable and uploads it to object storage. Metadata is updated so that the engine can locate valid files during subsequent reads and recovery.

The Virtual Lab website acts as the demonstration interface, allowing users to observe the process without needing to interact directly with the underlying storage implementation.

Technical Feasibility

Technical feasibility evaluates whether the required system can be implemented using available programming languages, libraries, storage services, and development tools.

Technology Feasibility

ComponentProposed technology or approach
Storage enginePython or Go
MemtableIn-memory dictionary or ordered structure
WALAppend-only persistent log
SSTablesSorted immutable data files
Object storageMinIO or an S3-compatible service
Metadata managementManifest or equivalent metadata file
Virtual Lab frontendWeb interface with interactive visualizations
TestingUnit tests, recovery tests and performance benchmarks

The specific stack can be finalized according to the team's familiarity and the Virtual Lab requirements.

Implementation Feasibility

The system can be implemented incrementally, beginning with basic key-value operations and progressing to persistence and cloud integration.

  • Stage 1: Implement PUT, GET, and DELETE using a Memtable.
  • Stage 2: Add the WAL and restart recovery.
  • Stage 3: Implement SSTable generation, indexing, and retrieval.
  • Stage 4: Integrate object storage and metadata management.
  • Stage 5: Implement compaction and handle obsolete values.
  • Stage 6: Connect the engine to the Virtual Lab interface and demonstrate its operations.

This staged approach allows each component to be tested independently before integration.

Technical Challenges

The primary challenges are ensuring that acknowledged writes can be recovered, identifying the latest value across multiple SSTables, handling failed uploads, and maintaining consistent metadata during flushes and compaction.

Object storage introduces additional network latency compared with local memory or local disk storage. Indexes, caching, and careful file organization may help reduce unnecessary remote requests.

Feasibility assessment: The project is technically feasible as a single-node academic prototype. Production-grade guarantees and distributed functionality would require substantially more implementation and testing.

Operational Feasibility

Operational feasibility determines whether the system can be run, demonstrated, tested, and maintained effectively.

The storage engine will expose basic key-value operations through an API or the Virtual Lab interface. Users will be able to insert records, retrieve values, delete keys, and observe how data moves from memory into persistent SSTable files.

The Virtual Lab will provide a visual representation of the storage engine's workflow, including WAL entries, Memtable contents, SSTable creation, object storage, and compaction. This will make the internal operations easier to understand and demonstrate.

Automated tests and logging will help developers identify errors, verify data integrity, and inspect recovery behaviour.

Feasibility assessment: Operational feasibility is high for a prototype, provided the setup, execution, recovery, and demonstration processes are properly documented.

Feasibility assessment: The project is achievable within a typical academic project schedule if the initial implementation remains focused on core storage functionality and an educational demonstration rather than a production database.

Risk Analysis

RiskImpactMitigation
Crash during a write or flushRecent data may become unavailableImplement WAL replay and recovery tests
Object storage upload failureSSTable may not be available for readsVerify uploaded files before publishing them in metadata
Incorrect version selectionOlder values may be returnedTrack record versions or sequence numbers
Compaction failureData loss or inconsistent file statePublish new files and update metadata safely before removing old files
High remote-read latencySlow GET operationsUse indexes, Bloom filters or caching where appropriate
Excessive SSTable growthIncreasing read overheadImplement basic compaction
Frontend and engine integration issuesVirtual Lab may display incorrect stateDefine API contracts and test integration early

The most important risk is maintaining consistency between persisted SSTables and metadata. The engine must ensure that files are safely uploaded and discoverable before deleting older files or treating the new state as committed.

Performance Evaluation Plan

The project will be evaluated using functional tests, recovery tests, and performance benchmarks.

MetricPurpose
Write throughputMeasures the number of writes processed per second
Read latencyMeasures the time required to retrieve a value
Write latencyMeasures the time required to complete a write
Recovery timeMeasures the time required to restore the engine after a restart
Read amplificationMeasures the amount of file or block access required per read
Write amplificationMeasures the total data written relative to logical user data
Storage overheadMeasures physical storage consumed relative to logical data size

Testing will include repeated updates to the same key, reads from older SSTables, deletion using tombstones, Memtable flushes, compaction, and simulated application crashes.

The results will help establish whether the engine behaves correctly and how object storage affects performance. Any performance claims will be based on measured results.

Expected Outcomes and Conclusion

The expected outcome is a functional prototype of an LSM-Tree storage engine integrated with object storage, accompanied by a Virtual Lab website for interactive demonstrations.

The project is expected to demonstrate:

  • Efficient write organization through a WAL and Memtable.
  • Generation and persistence of immutable SSTable files.
  • Retrieval of the latest valid values from stored data.
  • Basic compaction and management of obsolete records.
  • Recovery following supported crash scenarios.
  • Visualization of storage operations through the Virtual Lab.
  • Measured performance under selected workloads.

Conclusion: The proposed project is feasible within the scope of a single-node academic implementation. Its main challenges involve recovery correctness, metadata consistency, remote storage latency, and safe compaction. A modular implementation followed by systematic testing will make it possible to demonstrate the core principles of LSM-Tree storage over object storage.
